titleText.es: Dicen que no se puede argumentar contra los datos, ¿pero a qué viene esa actitud derrotista? Si le pones ganas, puedes argumentar contra CUALQUIER COSA.
titleText.en: They say you can't argue with results, but what kind of defeatist attitude is that? If you stick with it, you can argue with ANYTHING.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and English texts are the exact title attributes from the Spanish archive and official xkcd. OCR omitted the standalone Y that begins the final paragraph of the speech and all five printed dollar signs on the money bags; those source-checked units are restored explicitly. OCR also dropped several written accents that remain visible in the raster.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por mucho que
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Por begins the concessive connector por mucho que, used to say that a result holds no matter how much something happens.

example.es: Por mucho que preguntes, no lo sé.
example.en: No matter how much you ask, I do not know.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: much; however much (in por mucho que)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Within por mucho que, mucho supplies the idea of an unrestricted amount or degree.

example.es: Por mucho que corra, llega tarde.
example.en: No matter how much he runs, he arrives late.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por mucho que
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Que links por mucho to the action whose amount does not change the result.

example.es: Por mucho que insistas, diré que no.
example.en: No matter how much you insist, I will say no.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: they tell you; people may tell you
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After por mucho que, digan is a form of decir that leaves the amount or identity of what people say open. It is also the form used for a formal or plural command in other settings.

example.es: Por mucho que digan, mantendré mi decisión.
example.en: No matter what they say, I will keep my decision.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: stop; leave (command form for a familiar group)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dejéis is the form used when telling more than one familiar person not to do something. In dejar de plus another action, dejar means to stop that action.

example.es: No dejéis de practicar.
example.en: Do not stop practicing.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: lottery
failed
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Fracasado is the completed-action form of fracasar used after a form of haber.

example.es: El primer intento ha fracasado.
example.en: The first attempt has failed.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: given up; surrendered
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker, rendirse means to give up. Rendido is its completed-action form after haber.

example.es: No me he rendido.
example.en: I have not given up.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: work shifts
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A turno is a scheduled period of work. Turnos is plural.

example.es: Esta semana hago tres turnos.
example.en: This week I am working three shifts.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: double; twice as long or large
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dobles is plural because it describes more than one turno.

example.es: Trabajaron dos turnos dobles.
example.en: They worked two double shifts.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: tickets; lottery tickets
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Billete can mean a ticket, banknote, or travel pass. With de lotería, it means a lottery ticket.

example.es: Compró dos billetes de lotería.
example.en: She bought two lottery tickets.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: living; alive
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Viviente has the same singular form with a masculine or feminine noun.

example.es: Es la persona viviente de mayor edad.
example.en: She is the oldest living person.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: you all persevere; you all keep going
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Perseveráis is the present form used with vosotros, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain.

example.es: Si perseveráis, aprenderéis mucho.
example.en: If you all persevere, you will learn a lot.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: you all will succeed
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Triunfaréis keeps the full verb triunfar and adds -éis for a future action by vosotros, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain.

example.es: Con paciencia, triunfaréis.
example.en: With patience, you all will succeed.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: talks; presentations
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Charla can mean an informal conversation or a talk given to an audience. In the plural, charlas can refer to several presentations.

example.es: Habrá dos charlas esta tarde.
example.en: There will be two talks this afternoon.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: motivational; inspiring (feminine plural)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Motivadoras uses feminine plural -as to match charlas.

example.es: Escuchamos unas historias motivadoras.
example.en: We listened to some inspiring stories.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: survival

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that a result stays true no matter how much something happens?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use por mucho que, then a special verb form that leaves the amount or possibility open.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The special form is called the subjunctive. It often changes the ending: dicen becomes digan, and insistes becomes insistas. Por mucho que presents any amount of that action as unable to change the main result.

example.es: Por mucho que insistas, no cambiaré de opinión.
example.en: No matter how much you insist, I will not change my mind.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you tell a familiar group in Spain not to do something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put no or nunca before the negative command form for vosotros, such as no habléis or nunca salgáis.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Vosotros is the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain. For a regular -ar verb, replace -ar with -éis: hablar becomes habléis. For a regular -er or -ir verb, use -áis: comer becomes comáis and salir becomes salgáis, with some verbs also changing their stem.

example.es: No habléis todos a la vez.
example.en: Do not all speak at once.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone works a scheduled shift?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of hacer followed by un turno or turnos.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time. Turno names the scheduled period of work; an adjective can specify its type, as in turno nocturno or turno doble.

example.es: Marta hace el turno de noche.
example.en: Marta works the night shift.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What expression describes a living person whose experience is presented as evidence?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use prueba viviente, meaning “living proof.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Prueba names the evidence, and viviente emphasizes that a real living person embodies it. The expression does not by itself establish whether the evidence is reliable.

example.es: Ella es la prueba viviente de que se puede recuperar.
example.en: She is living proof that recovery is possible.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What is the name for judging a process only from the visible successes while overlooking the failures?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use sesgo de supervivencia for “survivorship bias.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Sesgo means a systematic distortion in judgment. Supervivencia identifies the distortion: the cases that remain visible are easier to study than the cases that disappeared or failed, so success can look more common than it really is.

example.es: Estudiar solo las empresas exitosas crea un sesgo de supervivencia.
example.en: Studying only successful companies creates survivorship bias.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: lotería · prueba viviente · sesgo de supervivencia
cardDefinitions.questionEn: Why is the lottery winner's motivational advice misleading?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: The visible winner treats persistence as proof while the many persistent losers are absent from the story.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is survivorship bias: attention goes to the rare successful case that can give a talk, not to the much larger set of people who followed the same strategy and lost. The money bags make the speaker's luck visible, while the caption identifies the reasoning error.

applications.explanationEn: Por mucho que opens the concession, and digan uses the special open-ended form for whatever people may say; os identifies the familiar group receiving those words.
Os marks the familiar plural listeners used with vosotros in Spain.
Nunca makes the instruction negative, and dejéis is the command form addressed to a familiar group.
The -éis ending is addressed to a familiar plural group in the Spain vosotros system.
Dejéis changes for the addressed group, de links it to comprar, and comprar stays in its unchanged -ar form.
He matches the speaker, and fracasado supplies the completed failure connected to the present story.
He matches the speaker, and rendido is the completed-action form; the preceding me belongs to rendirse, “to give up.”
Empecé gives the completed beginning, a links it to the activity, and hacer stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Hacer supplies the work action, and turnos names the scheduled work periods.
Dobles follows turnos in the neutral order for a descriptive adjective.
Dobles carries plural -es to match the plural noun turnos and has the same plural form for either gender.
Para introduces the purpose, and poder stays in its unchanged -er form.
Poder names the ability, and pagar remains in its unchanged -ar form.
Veis is the present form of ver for a familiar plural group in Spain.
Prueba names evidence, and viviente presents the speaker as a living embodiment of it.
Prueba names the claimed evidence, while de que introduces the claim supplied as its content; viviente describes that proof between them.
Si introduces the possible condition, perseveráis stays in an ordinary present form, and triunfaréis gives the future result.
The -áis ending marks an ordinary present action by a familiar plural group in Spain.
Triunfaréis keeps the complete verb triunfar and adds -éis for what the group will do.
The final -éis also identifies the familiar plural group addressed with vosotros.

Motivadoras uses feminine plural -as to match charlas.
Con éxito forms the conventional expression describing a successful person or result.
